newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Truce extended as Bangladesh peace talks begin.
newsitem.headline: Truce extended as Bangladesh peace talks begin.

text.p: Rebel leaders and the Bangladesh government on Saturday extended a truce until March 31 as they began talks aimed at ending a 23-year tribal insurgency in the southeastern Chittagong Hill Tracts, government officials said.
The current truce is due to expire on December 31.
The National Committee on the Hill Tracts affairs held a four-hour meeting with five leaders of the rebel Shanti Bahini (peace force) group at the town of Khagrachari Hill Tracts.

The meeting was, however, later adjourned until December 24, because of the illness of Jyotirindra Budhipriya Larma, chief of Parbatya Chattagram Jana Sanghati Samity (PCJSS), the political arm of Shanti Bahini, government officials said.
"The ceasefire was agreed at the meeting," one Khagrachari official told reporters.

The tribal guerrillas have been fighting a bush war for autonomy in the 5,500 sq mile (14,200 sq km) Hill Tracts, bordering India and Burma. They also want 300,000 Bengali-speaking settlers expelled from the area.
More than 8,500 rebels, soldiers and civilians have been killed since 1973.
The chief parliamentary whip of the ruling Awami League, Abul Hasnat Abdullah, led an eight-member government team which also included opposition MPs and local leaders.
Members from the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), however, did not turn up for the meeting, officials said.
The BNP lost to the Awami League, headed by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, in a general election last June.
"I am hopeful for the new government's intiative to end the lingering problems of the Hill Tracts," Larma told reporters after the meeting.
He refused however to give any guarantee that the much-violated truce would hold. "I can't assure about that. It is very much a relative matter," he said.

Larma denied any involvement of his men in the killing of 30 Bengali-speaking people last September and the more recent kidnapping of six government officials, who were later rescued by army commandos from a rebel hideout.
"The talks were held in a cordial and friendly atmosphere. We will meet again on Tuesday," Abdullah said.
Larma and his comrades were flown to the meeting by military helicopter from the remote Dudukchhari village bordering India's Tripura.
Tripura, where some 50,000 Hill Tracts residents, mostly members of Chakma tribe, have taken refuge, is also Larma's operations headquarters, counter-insurgeny officials said.
As many as 19 peace attempts have failed since 1985.
